# Measuring Intelligence Beyond Human Scale

**Authors:** Jerry Han Rafael Moschopoulos11footnotemark: 1 Ella Colby Vishrut Goyal Andrew Tu Kia Ghods Shirley Yu Mark Braverman Elad Hazan Princeton Superalignment ††thanks: Equal contribution.††thanks: We gratefully acknowledge contributions by Iris Yan and Connor Brown.

## Abstract

How can we measure intelligence beyond human capability? Human-authored benchmarks saturate, and above human capability, examiners may not know which tasks are both hard and verifiable. We argue that this difficulty is inherent to absolute-scale evaluation and propose a new paradigm based on relative measurement in which models generate public challenges that separate other systems. We develop a novel protocol that naturally scales with agent capabilities, requires no human-authored questions, and is also judge-free. We instantiate this framework across verifiable and open-ended, non-verifiable domains, illustrating how model-generated evaluation can continue to measure systems beyond the human frontier.

## 1 Introduction

How should intelligence be measured? The question is older than the study of artificial intelligence.

The modern scientific study of intelligence began with the work of Charles Spearman (Spearman, 1904). Spearman observed that individuals who performed well on one cognitive test tended also to perform well on many others, a phenomenon now known as the positive manifold. He hypothesized that these positive correlations were explained by a single latent factor, which he called general intelligence (g). This marked a fundamental shift from viewing intelligence as a collection of observable abilities to modeling it as a latent statistical variable inferred from observable behavior, laying the foundations of modern psychometrics. Interestingly, this is also the seed of factor analysis in statistics.

Most AI benchmarks inherit this psychometric structure. Systems are evaluated on tasks supplied by humans or environments fixed in advance: game environments, broad academic benchmarks and so on (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Srivastava and others, 2023; Liang et al., 2023; Chollet, 2019; White et al., 2025; Glazer et al., 2024; Phan and others, 2026; Kiela et al., 2021). This becomes a scaling problem at the frontier: benchmarks saturate, and new ones require humans to generate tasks that are difficult and verifiable. Above human expert level, the bottleneck is not only the number of questions, but the examiner’s ability to formulate discriminating questions.

#### Relative intelligence measurement.

A different starting point is relative measurement. Turing’s imitation game measures machine intelligence by comparison with human behavior before a human judge, rather than by an absolute score on a fixed test (Turing, 1950). Modern pairwise preference and arena methods similarly compare systems through judged interactions (Zheng et al., 2023; Chiang et al., 2024). These protocols point toward relative evaluation, but the tasks or judgments are still largely human-supplied. A notable exception is MathDuels (Xu et al., 2026), which explores model-generated mathematical challenges solved across the model population, as an evaluation primitive.

However, purely pairwise comparative protocols are vulnerable to failure modes that can make the resulting signal uninformative. A model may exploit private information, construct trapdoor tasks, or target one particular weakness of a single opponent rather than reveal a general capability distinction, see more details in section 3.1.

#### A different approach to measuring intelligence.

We propose a model-generated and separative approach to intelligence evaluation, which we call adversarial psychometrics. While classical psychometrics measures intelligence by how well subjects solve examiner-designed tasks, adversarial psychometrics evaluates a model’s ability to discover capability boundaries among other systems. We hypothesize that a model displays an important component of intelligence by constructing challenges that separate a population of solvers.

Our central move is to replace pairwise comparison with separative measurement. A challenge is evaluated not by whether it defeats one opponent, but by the variance in confidence it induces across a population of solvers. This shift rewards proposers for identifying distinctions across systems, rather than for exploiting specific weaknesses of a target. By evaluating systems on their capacity to discover such capability gaps, we obtain a richer statistical signal that can scale beyond the human frontier and can support sparse, or even judge-free adjudication.

Paper overview. The paper proceeds in three stages. First, we show that natural pairwise challenge protocols are fundamentally susceptible to private-information and trapdoor attacks, motivating a new one-to-many formulation. Second, we develop the separative psychometric framework, including its scoring rule, adaptive weighting, and judge-free adjudication mechanism. Third, we demonstrate the framework empirically across verifiable and open-ended, non-verifiable domains, showing that model-generated challenges discriminate between current systems without a semantic judge, correlating well with existing intelligence indices.

### 1.1 Relation to existing work

Psychometric and adaptive-testing models infer latent ability from responses to diagnostic items designed and administered by human examiners (Spearman, 1904; Rasch, 1960; Lord, 1980; van der Linden and Glas, 2010). Paired-comparison systems such as Bradley–Terry and Elo infer relative ratings from sparse pairwise outcomes. Methods such as TrueSkill extends probabilistic skill inference to multiplayer and team results and represents uncertainty. (Bradley and Terry, 1952; Elo, 1978; Herbrich et al., 2006). Modern AI evaluation has focused on benchmark construction, contamination resistance, frontier-level difficulty, dynamic task collection, and pairwise comparison, including MMLU, BIG-Bench, HELM, ARC, LiveBench, FrontierMath, Humanity’s Last Exam, Dynabench, MT-Bench, and Chatbot Arena (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Srivastava and others, 2023; Liang et al., 2023; Chollet, 2019; White et al., 2025; Glazer et al., 2024; Phan and others, 2026; Kiela et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2023; Chiang et al., 2024).

Language-Model-as-an-Examiner, Auto-Arena, and PeerRank automate question generation and evaluation while retaining semantic judgments as the source of their scores (Bai et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025; Margalit et al., 2026). LivingArena targets opponents’ weaknesses using a separate three-model judging panel (Chen et al., 2026). MathDuels (Xu et al., 2026) is particularly related to our work. It proposes a mathematical self-play benchmark in which models act as both problem posers and solvers. Our work shares the idea that task generation itself is a measurable capability, but differs in several respects: we study arbitrary domains rather than mathematics, develop a psychometric framework based on population separation against challenger-committed answers and investigate protocols that don’t require a semantic judge.

Relation to Scalable Oversight. The scalable oversight problem asks: how do we obtain reliable supervision for systems whose competence exceeds that of their supervisors (Amodei et al., 2016; Christiano et al., 2018). Existing proposed mechanisms include debate, in which models argue opposing answers before a weaker judge (Irving et al., 2018), weak-to-strong generalization, in which a weak supervisor elicits a stronger model’s latent ability (Burns et al., 2024), and sandwiching-style experiments, in which non-experts use model assistance on tasks evaluated against expert-defined answers (Bowman et al., 2022). Our work shares the same motivation: human evaluators may eventually be unable to author or verify sufficiently discriminating tasks. However, whereas scalable oversight seeks reliable supervision of individual systems, we focus on comparative measurement.

Relation to interactive proofs and complexity theory. There is also a conceptual connection to multi-prover interactive proofs (MIPs). In an MIP, a bounded verifier extracts reliable evidence by comparing the behavior of multiple provers; the theorem of Babai et al. (1991) that $\mathsf{MIP}=\mathsf{NEXP}$ demonstrated the remarkable power of such multi-agent verification. Our protocol is not an MIP in the formal sense: we do not provide completeness or soundness guarantees for a fixed language, nor do we assume a polynomial-time verifier. However, we have the shared idea that multiple agents can reveal information that a single agent cannot. Whereas MIPs use cross-prover consistency to verify mathematical claims, adversarial psychometrics uses cross-model disagreement to measure capability boundaries.

## 2 Background: Spearman’s general intelligence $g$

In the early 1900s, experimental psychologists were intrigued with the question of measuring human intelligence. Spearman followed Galton’s theories of intelligence but noted that Galton surprisingly failed to find associations between different performance metrics and common indicators of intelligence.

Spearman’s experiment. Spearman set out “to determine this Intelligence in a definite objective manner, and to discover means of precisely measuring it” (Spearman, 1904, p. 206). His clearest data came from a preparatory school for boys. He ranked the pupils by their results in the regular school examinations in Classics, French, English and Mathematics. He also tested their discrimination of pitch and obtained a ranking of musical ability for the 22 boys taking music lessons (Spearman, 1904, pp. 248–250, 270). Figure 1(a) is his table of correlations among these six measures for those 22 boys (Spearman, 1904, pp. 275, 291).

The positive manifold. Spearman observed that every correlation in the table is positive. A boy who ranks high in one subject tends to rank high in all of them, and even to hear finer differences in pitch. The entries are also orderly, falling steadily “as the eye travels either to the right or downwards,” a pattern Spearman called the hierarchy (Spearman, 1904, p. 275). He concluded that “all branches of intellectual activity have in common one fundamental function,” plus a specific element unique to each (Spearman, 1904, p. 284). He called it General Intelligence, later written $g$ .

## 3 Warm-up: pairwise intelligence tournaments

A natural first attempt is a pairwise intelligence tournament. Given two systems $i$ and $j$ , system $i$ is asked to produce a challenge that it can solve but system $j$ cannot. The challenge must be publicly specified and objectively resolvable. System $j$ then submits an answer under the same resource budget, and the outcome is recorded as a win for $i$ if $i$ ’s answer is correct and $j$ ’s answer is incorrect.

Over many such matches, the outcomes define a directed comparison graph: an edge $i\to j$ indicates that system $i$ found a challenge separating itself from system $j$ . In principle, this graph could be aggregated by any standard paired-comparison model, such as Bradley–Terry, Elo, or TrueSkill. For example, a Bradley–Terry model assigns each system a latent score $\theta_{i}$ and models

$$ \Pr(i\text{ beats }j)=\sigma(\theta_{i}-\theta_{j}). $$

Equivalently, one could maintain Elo-style online ratings from the same pairwise outcomes.

This gives a simple self-scaling measurement scheme: stronger systems should be able to find challenges that separate themselves from weaker systems, and the rating scale evolves with the population being measured. However, the pairwise formulation has fundamental flaws.

### 3.1 Caveats of pairwise protocols

The first difficulty is that this naive protocol rewards separation from a single opponent, and therefore creates incentives to exploit asymmetric information rather than capability. The simplest attack is a private-state question, such as “which bit am I thinking of?”

One might try to rule out such private or otherwise unfair questions. But the same problem can arise even in questions that appear fair. For example, a challenger can generate two large primes, publish their product, and ask for its factorization. Under the same resource budget the task may be hopeless for the solver, while the challenger has “solved” it only because it inserted the trapdoor during construction.

The common issue is that the challenger possesses information unavailable to the solver: in one case a private state, and in the other an algorithmic backdoor. Such separations need not reflect superior intelligence.

A second problem is adjudication. Even if private-information and trapdoor questions are formally disallowed, the protocol still requires someone to decide whether a challenge is admissible and whether its proposed resolution is correct. Without an external judge, the parties’ own reports can enforce agreement but not truth. Penalties for disagreement may induce the players to agree, but they cannot distinguish the truthful resolution from a biased one. Thus pairwise protocols either rely on external adjudication, which limits scalability, or remain manipulable.

The key observation is that private information and trapdoors are powerful mainly because the challenger is trying to fool a single opponent. If the same challenge is posed simultaneously to many independently trained systems, the reward depends on population disagreement rather than success against one solver. In an appropriately designed mechanism, shared uncertainty among players is indicative of an uninformative challenge and should yields no separation reward. This motivates the one-to-many protocol developed next.

## 4 The Basic Challenge Protocol

We call our novel ranking protocol SepaRank , and its basic description is as follows. A proposer submits a binary question with answers A and 11 1 Binary questions are without loss of generality. Any finite-answer question can be reduced to a sequence of binary questions (e.g., by asking for successive bits of the answer or by using a binary search over the answer space). Since our objective is to measure discriminative power rather than answer format, we restrict attention to binary questions for simplicity.. Each solver returns an answer and a confidence, equivalently a posterior probability $p_{i}$ assigned to answer A. The proposer is rewarded for inducing high variance in the values $\{p_{i}\}$ across solvers. No restriction is placed on the semantic content of the question. The question may be factual, mathematical, philosophical, subjective, future-contingent, or otherwise difficult to resolve externally.

The variance scoring changes the incentive relative to pairwise challenge protocols. The question “which bit am I thinking of?” no longer succeeds: a calibrated solver has no evidence and should report $p_{i}=\frac{1}{2}$ , so the variance is small. Likewise, a trapdoor-ed factoring instance does not help merely because the proposer generated the primes; the proposer anyways is not required to solve the problem, and if the problem is too hard, calibrated reports again concentrate near $\frac{1}{2}$ . The proposer succeeds only by finding questions that genuinely separate the audience. We conjecture that this discourages some uninformative challenges.

We use variance as the proposer objective for simplicity. Other separation objectives are also possible, such as the empirical entropy of the distribution of reports or a weighted Jensen–Shannon divergence, which measures how much information a report carries about which solver produced it.

### 4.1 Protocol

We evaluate systems in two roles: proposer and solver. The Separank protocol constists of $R$ rounds. For an $N$ -model panel, each round consists of $N$ matches. In match $i$ , model $i$ proposes one binary question and privately commits to an answer $y\in\{0,1\}$ . Every other model answers that question. All $N$ matches during round $r$ use the full information of the game of up to round $r-1$ .22 2 In practice, we truncate the protocol transcript to the past $5$ rounds for computational feasibility. However, model scores and standings are computed from round $1$ through $r-1$ . Current cross-match commitments and solver answers remain hidden until the round is complete. Only then are scores, weights, and public history updated. That way, matches can run in parallel.

Models use stable pseudonyms, which identify their answers and commitments throughout the entire game. Each solver $i$ reports a probability $p_{i}\in[0,1]$ that the committed answer is $1$ . Thus $p_{i}=1/2$ expresses equal uncertainty between the two answers, while values near $0$ or $1$ express confidence.

The proposer is rewarded for separating the solvers’ beliefs. For one question, let $p_{1},\ldots,p_{m}$ be the usable reports and let $w_{1},\ldots,w_{m}$ be their weights, normalized to sum to one. These are the round-start solver weights, renormalized over the solvers whose reports are usable. The proposer reward is

$$ \mu=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_{i}p_{i},\qquad P=4\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_{i}(p_{i}-\mu)^{2}. $$

This is the weighted population variance of the reported probabilities. With equal weights, it reduces to ordinary population variance. The factor $4$ places the reward in $[0,1]$ : it is zero when all solvers report the same probability, and reaches one when half the weight reports $0$ and half reports $1$ .

Variance captures the distinction between a question that separates the population and one that leaves everyone equally uncertain. For example, suppose a proposer asks, “which fair coin flip did I privately observe?” If no solver has information about the flip, each should report $1/2$ , giving the proposer zero reward. The proposer’s private knowledge alone therefore produces no separation in this case. A public question may instead give some solvers a basis for confidence while leaving others uncertain, producing positive variance. The objective rewards this difference in reported beliefs, rather than difficulty alone.

Solvers are scored separately against the author’s committed answer:

$$ L_{i}=(p_{i}-y)^{2}. $$

This proper scoring rule is Brier loss, and is smallest for an accurate, confident report and largest for a confidently incorrect one. For a fixed commitment, a solver minimizes its expected one-step loss by reporting its probability that $y=1$ (Brier, 1950; Gneiting and Raftery, 2007). The scoring target throughout the experiments is the commitment: even in verifiable domains, such as Python code challenges where execution could produce the correct answer, the solvers are scored against the proposer-committed bit. The two roles therefore ask different things of a model: find questions that separate the population, and forecast other authors’ committed answers.

Scores accumulate as two separate averages. A model’s proposer score, $\bar{P}$ , is the mean of its scored proposal rewards; its solver loss, $B$ , is the mean of its scored response losses. Higher $\bar{P}$ and lower $B$ are better. For the final ranking, we combine the two components with equal weight:

$$ J=\frac{\bar{P}+(1-B)}{2}. $$

This joint score is computed after play, separately for code and open-ended games. We also report both components. During play, adaptive weights depend only on past solver losses, as described in Section 4.2.

### 4.2 Adaptive solver weights

With equal weights, a proposer can continue to earn a high reward by separating the same groups of models. Once a question distinguishes the stronger solvers from the rest, variations of that question may keep producing disagreement without revealing differences among the stronger solvers themselves. We introduce adaptive weights to shift more of the measurement toward models that have performed well as solvers, and push proposers to keep separating the frontier. The weights determine how much each solver’s report contributes to the proposer’s variance reward. Every eligible model still solves every question from another author. A model with a small weight therefore retains the same opportunities to improve its solver score.

We begin with $3$ warmup rounds in which all $N$ active models have equal weight, $W_{i}=1/N$ . This gives the game an initial period of observation before past performance affects the proposer reward. After warmup, we use each model’s cumulative mean solver loss $B_{i}$ through the last completed round to set its weight for the next round:

$$ W_{i}=0.95\,\frac{\exp(-B_{i}/0.25)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}\exp(-B_{j}/0.25)}+\frac{0.05}{N}. $$

Lower solver loss gives greater weight. The denominator $0.25$ controls how sharply the weights respond to differences in loss: a smaller value would concentrate more weight on the best-performing solvers. The remaining $5\%$ is distributed uniformly, ensuring that every active model retains positive influence. Weights are recomputed from these cumulative losses after each completed round, For each question, we exclude its author and renormalize the weights over the usable solver reports, as in the variance formula of the protocol.

The intended effect is to make broad, already-established separations less rewarding as weight shifts toward the better forecasters. If most of the weight lies on solvers that give similar reports, disagreement confined to low-weight solvers contributes little to the reward. A question that separates the higher-weight solvers can contribute more. We conjecture that this encourages finer distinctions among reliable forecasters. The rule does not explicitly reward novelty, as this would require a separate definition of “novelty” and a judge to enforce it.

### 4.3 Resolution rules and optional adjudication

The SepaRank protocol separates the scoring mechanism from the resolution rule. In every round, solvers submit probabilities $p_{i}$ , the proposer is scored by the induced separation among those probabilities, and solvers are scored by a proper scoring rule against a resolved bit $y$ . The resolution rule specifies how $y$ is obtained.

In mechanically verifiable domains, $y$ may be determined by executing a program, checking a proof, or verifying a certificate. In this case solver loss measures accuracy with respect to an objective public truth. In non-verifiable domains, $y$ may instead be the proposer’s committed answer, along with a supplied rationale checked by a judge. In SepaRank, the proposer is allowed to commit any $y$ they wish, and the solver task becomes predicting the proposer’s committed resolution. The incentives this creates for the proposer, and the extent to which models exploit them, are measured in Section D.2. In experiments where we restrict the question scope to Python programs, we can verify the true $y$ by execution, and use it to understand the commitment behavior of proposers.

Although false commitments may increase disagreement in the short run, we conjecture that they should eventually erode trust. As a proposer becomes less reliable, calibrated solvers ought to hedge toward $\frac{1}{2}$ , reducing the proposer’s variance reward and creating a long-run incentive for honest commitments. The theoretical foundations of reputation, strategic stability, and conditions favoring semantically faithful commitments will be explored in future work.

Thus the proposer score always has the same meaning: it measures the ability to find questions on which the solver population separates. The solver score, however, is interpreted relative to the chosen resolution rule.

## 5 Experiments

We run SepaRank in two domains. In code games, proposers submit a Python program with a no-argument main() returning $0$ or $1$ . In open-ended games, they submit a yes/no question. In both, solvers predict the proposer’s private commitment. Executing code checks admissibility, but its output does not replace the proposer’s commitment $y$ , used to score the solvers. Open-ended questions receive format and length checks without a content judge.

We run 10 independent games per domain, each lasting 20 rounds and containing the same ten models from five providers (Table 1). All models use their provider’s low-effort reasoning setting. This was chosen to reduce API expenses and the runtime of the experiments. Every model proposes once per round, and all 9 peers solve each valid challenge. Players have stable pseudonyms within a game, and the current author’s pseudonym is disclosed during a match. Prompts provide to the players the full protocol details (scoring rules, constraints, cumulative standings, etc.) and the history of the last 5 completed rounds, which includes proposed questions with their authors and commitments, and players’ answers. The history is truncated to 5 rounds to reduce API expenses. Appendix B gives the full setup, and Appendix C reproduces the prompts.

Within each game, let $P$ be the mean proposer reward and $B$ the mean solver Brier loss. We report solver skill $S=1-B$ and joint score $J=(P+S)/2$ , so higher $P$ , $S$ , and $J$ are better. Unless stated otherwise, intervals are pointwise $95\%$ percentile intervals from $50{,}000$ whole-game bootstrap resamples, retaining all players and both roles together.

### 5.2 Comparison with external benchmarks

We compare SepaRank with ten individual benchmarks, the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, and an estimated benchmark factor $\widehat{g}$ for the same ten model releases (Artificial Analysis, 2026). Figure 6 reports Spearman correlations separately for proposer reward, solver skill, and joint score. The Index correlations are $0.900$ , $0.900$ , and $0.936$ for code, and $0.790$ , $0.717$ , and $0.851$ for open-ended games.

Agreement varies across benchmarks: the code joint score correlates $0.915$ with Terminal-Bench 4.0, but $-0.006$ with SciCode. We use all ten models and assign midranks to ties.

We also estimate a benchmark $g$ using the one-factor model in Section 2. We standardize each of the ten component benchmarks across the ten models, fit their off-diagonal correlations by minimum-residual factor analysis, and obtain a regression factor score $\widehat{g}$ for each model. Correlations with $\widehat{g}$ are $0.903$ , $0.758$ , and $0.915$ for code, and $0.721$ , $0.527$ , and $0.758$ for open-ended games, in proposer, solver, and joint order.

We observe that our proposed SepaRank scores correlate positively with virtually all the individual benchmark measures of model capability. In addition, SepaRank scores correlate much higher with compositive measures of model capability (AA Intelligence Index), as well as the estimated spearman $\hat{g}$ from these benchmarks. Our proposed mechanism thus successfully attains our desired goal.

In Appendix D we explore the score dynamics of games, the false commitment behavior of proposers in the verifiable code setting, and the effect on attained scores of obscuring the proposer’s name in a match.

## 6 Conclusion

We proposed an adversarial tournament protocol for measuring advanced AI capabilities. Models are evaluated by their ability to generate challenges that separate the forecasts of peer solvers. The resulting separations and ability to solve the challenges induce a ranking of the agents that we call SepaRank . The underlying thesis is that when human examiners can no longer reliably design frontier-level tests, evaluation itself must become model-generated and incentive compatible.

As for further work, the protocol described induces machine-generated questions and knowledge that can be further used for post-training and self-improvement. An important direction is to ensure diverse and effective generation of questions as well as correct answers at the frontier of knowledge.

After warmup, let $B_{i}$ be player $i$ ’s mean Brier loss over all its scored solver replies in completed rounds. The next round uses

$$ W_{i}=0.95\,\frac{\exp(-B_{i}/0.25)}{\sum_{j}\exp(-B_{j}/0.25)}+\frac{0.05}{N}, $$

where the sum is over the $N$ active players. Uniform weights are also used if any active player has no scored solver observations. Lower loss gives a solver more influence on the proposer reward, while the uniform component keeps every active solver’s weight positive.

For a particular proposal, the author’s own weight is excluded and the remaining weights are renormalized over usable replies. Writing these weights as $w_{i}$ and the corresponding forecasts as $p_{i}$ , the reward is

$$ \mu=\sum_{i}w_{i}p_{i},\qquad P=4\sum_{i}w_{i}(p_{i}-\mu)^{2}. $$

The joint score reported after play is $J=(\overline{P}+1-\overline{B})/2$ . It is computed separately for code and open-ended games and is not used to update weights or determine what any player sees during play.

Reported condition-level scores give each replicate game equal weight. Score intervals are pointwise 95% percentile intervals from 50,000 whole-game bootstrap resamples. Each resampled game retains all models and both roles together. For the author-withheld ablation, resampling retains the five matched game pairs. Its intervals enumerate all $5^{5}$ ordered bootstrap resamples of those pairs.

### B.3 What players see

All matches in a round use the same round-start history, standings, and weights. Results from that round are published together after every match has finished. A turn therefore cannot see another player’s current commitment or report. Within a match, the commitment is fixed before the solver replies are collected.

Every player sees the cumulative standings and the last five completed rounds of full challenges, commitments, solver reports, and results. Earlier rounds still contribute to the cumulative scores and weights. Past authors are identified by pseudonym. Each turn is otherwise a fresh request: no private conversation from earlier turns is supplied. A format retry retains the preceding reply within that turn.

The author-withheld ablation removes only the explicit current-author attribution and informs proposers of that change. It retains the attributed public history and cumulative standings. Thus the ablation tests the value of the explicit author label, not whether authorship can ever be inferred from content or history.

### B.4 Challenge validation and execution

Code. A submission contains a Python program and a separate final ANSWER: 0 or ANSWER: 1 line. The parser selects the last complete fenced block tagged python, py, or python3. The program must be at most 8,000 characters and define a top-level, synchronous main() with no arguments, returning an actual integer 0 or 1. The program must pass static checks and terminate in two independent executions with the same returned bit.

The recorded runtime was CPython 3.12.6 on Darwin arm64, with PYTHONHASHSEED=0 and 64-bit siphash13 hashing. Each execution had a 30-second wall-clock limit and a four-second total process CPU limit, comprising two configured seconds and two seconds of startup allowance. A 256 MiB address-space limit was configured. The import allowlist and forbidden names and attributes are reproduced in Appendix C. They exclude filesystem and network access, dynamic execution, reflection, and private-state input. Class patterns may use only permitted public keyword attributes, with no positional class patterns. Execution establishes validity and records the returned bit but does not replace the author’s commitment as the scoring target.

Open-ended questions. A submission is a JSON object containing a question and a commitment in $\{0,1\}$ . The question must be nonempty and at most 2,000 characters after trimming outer whitespace. The prompt asks for a yes/no question with one objectively resolvable answer shared by all readers, independent of their identities, private states, and the hidden commitment. The harness checks the format, length, and binary commitment, without using a semantic judge.

### B.5 Parsing and failure rules

A solver is asked for a JSON object with a finite numerical p_one field. The parser tolerates surrounding prose and JSON fences, selects the last parsed object with that top-level field, and gives JSON-fenced objects precedence. Finite values outside $[0,1]$ are clipped to that interval. A parsing failure permits one format retry. If a question commitment is expressed as an equivalent Boolean, binary number, or recognized yes/no string, it is normalized to 0 or 1. If a code submission contains a program but lacks a commitment, the retry requests only the commitment and retains the program. A program that fails static or execution checks receives no repair attempt.

An invalid proposal receives reward $-1$ and is included in the proposer’s mean. A solver reply that remains unparseable after the retry receives Brier loss 1 when the target is available, but does not enter the variance calculation. A valid proposal with fewer than five usable replies is unscored for the proposer. Communication or infrastructure failures produce neither invented answers nor player penalties.

At a round boundary, a player is held out if it has at least six cumulative author or solver turns and at least half are failed turns. A holdout pauses the game before further rounds. No player met this holdout rule in the reported experiment.

### D.2 Commitments and executed outputs

Code games let us compare each private commitment with the program’s executed output. Among $1{,}943$ valid proposals, $463$ commitments differ from that output ( $23.8\%$ ; $95\%$ interval $[21.5\%,26.3\%]$ ). Figure 8 shows substantial variation across models. Astra and Fable, the two highest-ranked models, have the lowest mismatch rates: $2/200$ ( $1.0\%$ ) and $8/178$ ( $4.5\%$ ). Grok 4.5 has the highest, $100/191$ ( $52.4\%$ ).

The same figure compares mean proposer rewards on consistent and mismatching proposals. Among valid proposals, mismatches receive higher mean rewards for eight of the ten models; for Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, the means are $0.517$ versus $0.028$ , and for Sonnet, $0.349$ versus $0.054$ . Thus, mismatches can accompany strong separation, while the highest overall rankings coexist with low mismatch rates. These are descriptive associations since the variance reward has no direct dependence on the committed bit, and a mismatch alone does not establish intentional deception. An underlying association may arise through game dynamics, in which solvers respond differently to the observed commitment tendency of a proposer.

### D.3 Withholding the current author

The default protocol lets solvers use a pseudonymous author’s earlier behavior when predicting its next commitment. To examine this information channel, we run 5 open-ended games in which solvers are not told the current author’s pseudonym. We compare them with the first 10 rounds of 5 author-disclosed games sharing their seeds and pseudonym assignments.

Figure 9 reports paired differences, withheld minus disclosed, at this common ten-round horizon.
